children: What happened?

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session as AI-linked shares continued to pull back. Anthropic slid more than 10% following its debut, failing to revive confidence in the sector's spending boom.

Investors had looked to Anthropic's record $81.3 billion initial public offering and Nvidia's quarterly earnings beat under interim CEO Colette Kress to steady sentiment following Jensen Huang's resignation, CNBC reported. Instead, Anthropic's retreat toward its $83 offer price echoed Seaport Research warnings, covered by CNBC, that its valuation demands much faster revenue growth.

Separately, Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned against delaying rate hikes ahead of an expected December increase. Compounding the concerns, President Donald Trump threatened penalties on overseas U.S. data-center builds as new Commerce Department export-licensing rules weighed on chipmakers.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.
Among others, the following stocks were impacted:
Analog semiconductors company SiTime fell 10%.
Semiconductor manufacturing company Camtek fell 9.2%.
Analog semiconductors company Vishay Intertechnology fell 10.1%. Is now the time to buy Vishay Intertechnology?

children: Zooming in on Vishay Intertechnology

Vishay Intertechnology’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 62 moves greater than 5% over the last year. But moves this big are rare even for Vishay Intertechnology and indicate this news significantly impacted the market’s perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 4 days ago when the stock dropped 4% on the news that Federal Reserve Governor Michael S. Barr warned of debt and overinvestment risks in the artificial intelligence buildout and the U.S. Commerce Department tightened export rules on overseas AI compute hubs.

In remarks published by the Federal Reserve, Barr cautioned that on-balance-sheet debt at the seven largest AI firms is set to surpass $800 billion by year-end alongside more than $3 trillion in nominal off-balance-sheet leases, energy contracts, and collateral guarantees, while rising capital costs for externally funded builders echo the late-1990s telecom boom.

Simultaneously, CNBC reported Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security will require export licenses for advanced chips bound for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil to block Chinese compute leasing. For analog chipmakers, which supply power-management and signal-processing components for data-center and energy infrastructure, tighter export licensing on overseas compute hubs and any financing-driven slowdown in debt-funded AI buildouts could curb hardware demand and weigh on sector sentiment, even if those mature chips are not the direct target of the rules.

Vishay Intertechnology is up 45.6% since the beginning of the year, but at $22.27 per share, it is still trading 65.7% below its 52-week high of $64.90 from June 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Vishay Intertechnology’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $1,021.

Nvidia’s chips cost a hundred grand. The connectors that make them work cost even more. One company makes them all.

Every AI server needs specialized infrastructure the chip companies don’t make. High-speed cables. Power connectors. Thermal sensors. This 90-year-old company built a monopoly on it. The AI boom just started. This stock is still flying under the radar.
